name: Frankish Kingdom (Merovingians)
summary: The Frankish kingdom created by Clovis I, who united the Franks, defeated the Romans and Visigoths in Gaul and became Catholic; ruled by his Merovingian family until the Carolingians took the crown in 751.

knownFor.label: Battle of Tours
knownFor.note: Charles Martel stops an Umayyad raid.

location.value: Gaul (modern France) and western Germany, with courts at Paris, Soissons, Reims and Orléans.

terrain.value: Plains, forests and river valleys, including the Seine, Loire, Rhine and Meuse.

climate.value: Temperate, with mild, wet weather across most of Gaul.

resources.value: Farmland, forests, iron, salt and river transport.

disasters.value: The plague that began in 541 and famines caused great loss of life.

population.value: The page gives no total; the historian Yitzhak Hen holds the Gallo-Roman population was far greater than the Frankish, especially south of the Seine.

urbanisation.value: Mostly rural; a few walled towns and a royal or ducal capital.

disease.value: Plague outbreaks, above all the Black Death (1347–51).

migration.value: Franks settled among the Gallo-Romans, mostly in the north, while Romans stayed on in the south.

economicBase.value: Trade declined with the fall of Rome and agricultural estates were mostly self-sufficient; remaining international trade was dominated by Middle Eastern merchants.

tradeRoutes.value: Rivers (Rhine, Seine); trade with Anglo-Saxon England.

wealth.value: Wealth came from land, tribute and plunder, and kings gave land to loyal warriors.

moneyAndTax.value: Gold, then silver coins; declining Roman taxes.

inequality.value: Nobles and clergy above peasants, many of them serfs.

governmentType.value: After Clovis died in 511 his kingdom was partitioned among his four sons and stayed divided until 679 apart from four short reunifications; the main divisions were Austrasia, Neustria, Burgundy and Aquitaine.

keyRulers.value: Childeric I died in 481; Clovis won at Tolbiac against the Alemanni in 496 and adopted Nicene Christianity, beat the Visigoths at Vouillé in 507 and died in 511; mayors of the palace held real power, Charles Martel ruled from 737 to 741, and Pepin the Short deposed Childeric III in 751 with Pope Zachary’s blessing.

succession.value: After Clovis’s death in 511 the kingdom was partitioned among his four sons; it stayed divided until 679 except for four short periods.

institutions.value: Mayors of the palace held real power by the 700s.

stability.value: Mayors of the palace held real power; the Austrasians triumphed at Tertry in 687.

eliteConflict.value: Rivalry between the kingdoms of Austrasia and Neustria, and among the sons of each king, who divided the realm.

majorWars.value: Battle of Tours in 732, where Charles Martel’s Franks defeated the Moors.

territoryChange.value: Clovis and his sons took most of Gaul by 537, including Burgundy and Provence.

alliancesRivals.value: Clovis’s conversion to Catholic Christianity won the support of the Gallo-Roman bishops, and later the popes; the Visigoths and Byzantines were rivals.

inventions.value: No major inventions are recorded, though Merovingian goldsmiths made fine jewellery.

scienceEducation.value: Monastery schools preserved some learning and writing.

openness.value: Open to trade; closed to rival faiths at times.

communicationTransport.value: Roman roads, rivers and coastal shipping continued to be used.

religion.value: Christianity came to the Franks through contact with Gallo-Roman culture and spread further through monks, the most famous missionary being Columbanus.

languageWriting.value: Latin for government and the Church; Frankish was the language of the ruling warriors.

artsArchitecture.value: Garnet-inlaid jewellery, illuminated manuscripts and early churches such as the Baptistery in Poitiers.

socialStructure.value: Kings, nobles, free Franks, Gallo-Romans, slaves.

sharedIdentity.value: Loyalty to the king and Church mixed Frankish and Roman customs.

dailyLife.value: Village farming; bread, porridge and beer or wine.

ideasReligions.value: The spread of monasteries, such as those founded by Columbanus, strengthened Christianity.

colonisation.value: The Franks took over Roman Gaul after the empire’s collapse.

riseSignals.value: Named for Merovech, father of Childeric I (died 481); Clovis I (died 511) converted to Nicene Christianity, dated 496 by Gregory of Tours.

peakPeriod.value: Under Dagobert I (629–639), the last strong Merovingian king.

declineSignals.value: “Do-nothing kings” (rois fainéants) after 639, with real power held by the palace mayors.

outcome.value: In 751 Pepin the Short deposed the last king, Childeric III, and began the Carolingian dynasty.

overallCertainty.value: Main events are known from chronicles and charters; population figures are estimates.
